summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
summary.describes_version: as explained in the linked explanatory memorandum
sentences: This bill would connect the news-business register with the proposed News Journalism Payment Scheme.
The Australian Communications and Media Authority would have to tell the department administering payments about specified changes in registered businesses and corporations.
The notifications would help the department assess eligibility and payment entitlements under the separate payments bill.
changes: Requires notifications when news businesses or corporations are registered, endorsed or have those arrangements revoked.
Requires relevant notifications about ownership changes or failure to meet registration requirements.
Requires notifications when news sources are added to or removed from a registered business.
Specifies information that notifications must contain, including the event date and relevant business, source and contact details.
summary.affected: Registered news businesses, their corporations, the communications regulator and the department administering journalism payments are affected.

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill sets up a scheme to distribute money collected from digital platforms to news organisations that produce public interest journalism.
The Secretary of the relevant department would run the scheme, deciding who gets payments based on how many editorial workers a news corporation employs.
Payments would be made twice a year, starting in March and September, if enough funds are available.
changes: Creates the News Journalism Payment Scheme to distribute revenue from the News Bargaining Incentive.
Requires news corporations to maintain their eligible editorial capacity or face recovery of excess funding.
Establishes a compliance framework with civil penalties for false information or non-compliance.
Allows the Secretary to give grants to ineligible organisations like the Australian Associated Press.
Sets up internal merits review of key decisions, with further review possible by the Administrative Review Tribunal.
Gives the Minister rule-making power for scheme details, subject to parliamentary disallowance.
summary.affected: Eligible news corporations, their editorial workers, small to medium publishers, regional and remote news outlets, and the Australian Associated Press.

divisions.question: Sharon Claydon In accordance with standing order 133, I shall now proceed to put the question on the amendment to the motion moved for the second reading of the News Journalism Payments Bill of 2026, on which a division was called for and deferred in accordance with the standing order. No further debate is allowed. The question is that the amendment moved by the honourable member for Lindsay be agreed to.

Anthony Albanese Right around the world, the organisations that invest in the news are losing revenue to the tech platforms that use their work. Television, radio and newspaper newsrooms, including the National Press Gallery here in Parliament House, have felt the effects through budget cuts, staff reductions and increased workloads. I want to say to Australia's journalists, news producers, editors, photographers and videographers: we have your back. The sustainability of our news sector must be addressed, and it must be addressed urgently, because a healthy news sector is essential for a flourishing democracy. Without broadly accepted objective facts, reasoned debate becomes impossible. We talk not to each other but past each other. It makes it harder for us to maintain our great Australian sense of optimism. We literally stop being on the same page. This legislation will help keep 28 million Australians on that same page. In a world where lies are routinely spread by bad actors, sometimes by images that are literally not real, truthful and accurate news is more important than ever. In its absence, debate is too often replaced by anger, discourse by shouting, democratic discussion by abuse and cooperation by division. As we all know, this trend, tragically, is global. But we can counter it. With this legislation, Australia is now once again taking leadership on making digital technology work for people—making sure that platforms make an appropriate contribution to the news that they rely on and from which they make enormous profits. We are showing the way to support the fourth estate, and, once again, we offer our policy as a model to the democratic world. The News Bargaining Incentive is world-leading legislation that will help keep our media sector vibrant and sustainable into the future. It is bipartisan, and it is strong. speeches.brief: Speaking for the Coalition on the News Journalism Payments Bill 2026, argued the government's replacement for the Coalition's news media bargaining code will deliver less support to journalism, between $200 million and $250 million versus the roughly $250 million a year the original code generated, criticised gaps in revenue verification and grant transparency, and moved a second reading amendment expressing no confidence that the new scheme improves on the Coalition's code.

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would restrict defence supplies, investments and trade connected with specified international crimes or illegal settlements, and introduce reporting on genocide risks.
It would require covered entities to publish annual genocide statements about their operations and value chains, with civil and criminal consequences for serious reporting failures.
Trade restrictions would target goods and services associated with illegal settlements in occupied territories, while allowing imports from lawful people and entities in lawful settlements.
changes: The minister would have to refuse, revoke or modify defence permits covering prohibited activities.
Defence supply prohibitions would extend to transactions that do not require permits.
The Future Fund, charities and superannuation entities would face divestment duties and restrictions on investments linked to illegal settlements or genocide risk.
A publicly accessible register would record defence supplies and ministerial decisions, subject to limits on redacting sensitive information.
An Australian Anti-Genocide Commissioner would be established once separate legislation provided funding.
summary.affected: Defence suppliers, importers, the Commonwealth, covered businesses, universities, charities, superannuation entities and the Future Fund are affected.

/bills/au-federal-s1515.json.title: Military Rehabilitation and Compensation Amendment (Veterans’ Allied Health Care) Bill 2026
/bills/au-federal-s1515.json.short_title: Military Rehabilitation and Compensation Amendment (Veterans’ Allied Health Care) Bill 2026

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would protect specified allied health treatment and compensation entitlements for veterans and dependants from spending caps and reviews triggered by expenditure thresholds.
It would prohibit required gap payments and restrictions imposed solely or substantially because aggregate treatment costs approach or exceed a set amount, while preserving clinical controls.
The protections would apply from the day after Royal Assent to treatment and compensation entitlements arising before or after commencement, without reopening earlier final amounts.
changes: An inclusive definition of allied health professionals would allow regulations to add professions without removing those expressly covered.
The Treatment Principles could not use spending thresholds as the sole or substantial reason to interrupt allied health care.
Compensation pathways would be protected from aggregate caps, while a new provision would allow reimbursement to be limited to actual treatment costs.
Regulations could extend protection to additional statutory treatment and compensation pathways.
summary.affected: Eligible veterans, dependants, allied health practitioners and the Military Rehabilitation and Compensation Commission are affected.

/bills/au-federal-r7378.json.short_title: Defence Amendment (Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence) Bill 2025

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would create a new parliamentary committee to oversee Australia's defence agencies.
The committee would have up to 13 members and could request information, documents, and briefings, but would be restricted from publicly disclosing sensitive information without ministerial approval.
The bill includes criminal offences for unauthorised use or disclosure of protected information by committee members, their staff, and other authorised parliamentarians.
changes: Creates the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence within the Defence Act 1903.
Gives the committee power to review, monitor, and report on Australian defence agencies, excluding certain intelligence organisations.
Imposes restrictions on public proceedings and disclosure of protected information, with ministerial certificates overriding disclosure requirements.
Establishes criminal offences for unauthorised use or disclosure of protected information.
summary.affected: Australian defence agencies, including the Australian Defence Force, Department of Defence, and Department of Veterans' Affairs, as well as committee members, their staff, and other authorised parliamentarians.

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the exposure draft text; not the record
summary.describes_version: as released for consultation on 8 September 2026
sentences: This exposure draft would rewrite Part 2 of the Online Safety Act 2021 to impose a digital duty of care: anyone who provides or controls an online service would have to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment for people in Australia and for children in particular.

Providers would have to manage design features such as recommender systems, endless feeds and engagement feedback, run written risk assessments at least once a year and act on them, with the eSafety Commissioner able to issue formal warnings and remedial directions and a civil penalty of up to 60,000 penalty units for a breach.

It would also let the Commissioner order app stores and search engines to remove apps and links used to make fake nude material within 24 hours, open a data access scheme for approved researchers, and repeal the industry codes and standards of the online content scheme, with the duty of care commencing 12 months after assent.
changes: Replaces the objects of the Online Safety Act 2021 with a duty on persons responsible for online services to ensure a safe online environment (Schedule 2, item 1).

Defines online services broadly: social media, messaging, designated internet services, hosting, search, app stores, equipment suppliers and services that generate and share AI material; the Minister may exempt low-risk or little-used services (section 25A).

Lists seriously harmful material and conduct (section 25C) and material harmful to children (section 25D), and names recommender, logged-in, endless-feed, feedback and time-limited features as having negative behavioural impacts, which social media services must not operate for Australians under 16 (sections 25B, 25F and 25G).

Requires written risk assessments at least annually and before any change that could add risk, kept for six years and produced to the Commissioner within 30 days; the Minister may require user empowerment tools (sections 26 and 26A). Lawful private communications between consenting adults are excepted.
Sets civil penalties of 60,000 penalty units for breaching the duty or a remedial direction, and 6,000 for failing to run required complaint and dispute processes (sections 26B, 26D and 26F).

Adds a 24-hour removal notice for apps and websites predominantly used to generate fake nude material (Schedule 1, section 86B), a data access scheme for approved researchers including permission to use sock puppet identities for research (sections 205B to 205H), and repeals the online content scheme's industry codes and standards (Schedule 3).
summary.affected: Providers and controllers of online services used in Australia, including social media, messaging, search, app stores and generative AI services; children under 16 on social media; approved researchers; and the eSafety Commissioner.
